The FOMC’s October 2019 decision to cut the target range to 1.50–1.75% and to employ T‑bill purchases and repo operations to maintain ample reserves is consistent with evidence that monetary policy can support real activity when inflation is below target (Sims 1992; B. Friedman; Taylor 1983; McCallum and Nelson 1999). With market-based inflation compensation low and longer-run expectations little changed, the literature on inflation targeting and expectations anchoring suggests limited credibility risk from easing when inflation is under the symmetric 2% objective (Svensson; Galí, Gertler, and López‑Salido on the expectations‑based Phillips curve). At the same time, the statement’s emphasis on weak business fixed investment aligns with findings that financing constraints amplify cutbacks in capex and inventories, a channel monetary easing can partially offset by improving liquidity and lowering the cost of funds (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994). Netting these forces, the tone is cautiously positive—supportive of continued expansion, but mindful of downside risks from soft investment and trade.
